newsitem.title: USA: Gingrich appeals to Republicans to re-elect him.
newsitem.headline: Gingrich appeals to Republicans to re-elect him.

text.p: Newt Gingrich's campaign to be re-elected speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives despite admitted ethics violations took a sharp blow on Monday, the eve of the vote, when a senior Republican urged him to step aside.

Gingrich made no comment as he headed into a crucial meeting with his colleagues on Monday evening to try to nail down re-election. It was his first face-to-face encounter with House Republicans since they nominated him by acclamation last November to be speaker in the new Congress that convenes on Tuesday.

Gingrich earlier met in his office with Republican House leaders and former Republican Leader Robert Michel, who retired from Congress two years ago but had been mentioned as a possible interim replacement as speaker. Under the U.S. Constitution the speaker does not have to be a House member, although all of them have been.
Budget Committee Chairman John Kasich of Ohio said: "At the end of the day, we'll be fine. I don't think we ought to run for the hills when the going gets tough."

In a statement issued earlier, Representative James Leach of Iowa, chairman of the House Banking Committee, said Gingrich was too tainted by ethics breaches to hold a post as prestigious and powerful as the speakership.
The statement sharply increased the pressure on Gingrich as he prepared to fight for his political future.

Leach's office said he would "vote for another Republican" in the speakership election on Tuesday -- the first such crack in the ranks of leading House Republicans. There was no indication who his choice might be.
Before Leach only Representative Michael Forbes of New York, a junior member about to start his second congressional term, had said he would not vote for Gingrich.
However some other members were expected to make up their minds only after hearing Gingrich speak.

A CNN/Gallup poll conducted over the weekend showed 65 percent of those asked believed Gingrich should be replaced as speaker. The poll found that 51 percent of Republicans believed he should be replaced. That finding had a margin of error plus or minus 5 percent.

In a three-page statement, Leach said in part: "The occupant of this position must be free of any shadow concerning allegiance to the law or to the truth. Accordingly for the country's sake I have concluded that the most responsible course of action for the speaker is to step down and for the members to choose another leader for the House."

Gingrich admitted on December 21 that he had brought discredit to the House by not doing enough to prevent the use of tax-exempt donations in a partisan political activity -- in this case a college course he taught titled "Renewing American Civilisation" -- and by misleading ethics committee investigators looking into the matter.

A sore point among Democrats and some other Gingrich critics is that the speakership vote will take place one day before the ethics committee begins the process of considering punishments for him. That process is scheduled to run about two weeks before the full House renders its decision.
Many expected the punishment would be a reprimand, a penalty the commmittee's rules say is appropriate for serious offences but less grave than expulsion or censure.
Leach is widely respected among his colleagues as a thoughtful, principled member of the House, but one who often steers an independent course.
As banking chairman, he led a House investigation into the Whitewater business and ethics controversy involving President Bill Clinton and Hillary Rodham Clinton.

Leach drew a parallel to Clinton's troubles on Monday, saying, "It is self-evident that a critical way for the Republican Party to contrast itself with this administration is to set uncompromising ethical standards and insist on appropriate and timely accountability for its members."
